19 
the forecast billing determinants derived from the sales forecast provided

by the Company's Gas Load Forecast (“GLF”) Panel.  Details of the Rate

Q. 
Please explain how the Company developed its base delivery revenue 
1 
forecast for the Rate Year. 
2 
A. 
For firm and non-firm sales and transportation service classifications (SC 1, 
3 
2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19), the base delivery revenue forecast was 
4 
developed based on the forecast average number of customers and 
5 
deliveries.  Deliveries were allocated to the usage blocks within each service 
6 
class using a three-year average percentage of actual billed block usage to 
7 
allocate sales.  To normalize for the impacts of the COVID pandemic, the 
8 
Company used historic billed block usage for calendar years 2019, 2021 
9 
and 2022 (excluding calendar year 2020) to calculate the historic three-year 
10 
average percentages.  
11 
 
12 
Q. 
Has the Company used a three-year average percentage of actual billed 
13 
block usage to allocate sales to the various blocks in prior rate case 
14 
proceedings? 
15 
A. 
No.  In previous rate case proceedings, the Company has used an ogive 
16 
analysis to allocate the usage blocks within each service classification.  
17 
  
18 


--- Page 18 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 15 of 74 
 
Q. 
Why did the Company use a three-year average percentage of actual 
1 
billed block usage (as opposed to an ogive analysis) to allocate sales to 
2 
the various blocks? 
3 
A. 
In accordance with the Joint Proposal in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate 
4 
Cases, the Company met with Department of Public Service Staff (“Staff”) 
5 
to discuss potential options for developing a methodology to normalize data 
6 
prior to commencing its ogive process.  During this meeting, the Company 
7 
and Staff concluded that the Company would compare the results of an 
8 
ogive analysis to a historic three-year average percentage of actual billed 
9 
block usage by rate code.  After reviewing the results of this comparison, 
10 
the Company and Staff determined that both methodologies provided 
11 
similar results when applied to a revenue forecast.  Because the two 
12 
methodologies provided similar results and the historic average is a simpler 
13 
methodology, the Company proposes to allocate the delivery forecast by 
14 
block by rate code using a historic three-year average percentage of actual 
15 
billed block usage in its revenue forecast.    
16 
  
17 
Q. 
Please explain how the revenue forecast for the electric generators was 
18 
developed. 
19 
A. 
The electric generator revenue forecast was developed by multiplying each 
20 
customer’s actual usage for 12-months ending October 2022 by their 
21 


--- Page 19 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 16 of 74 
 
applicable current transportation charge, daily balancing service demand 
1 
charge, value added charge, and gross revenue tax rates effective October 
2 
2022.  Each customer’s applicable annual minimum bill obligation was then 
3 
compared against the customer’s calculated revenue forecast using actual 
4 
charges and historic usage as described previously.  If a customer’s annual 
5 
minimum bill obligation was greater than its revenue forecast, the 
6 
customer’s annual minimum bill obligation was used in the electric 
7 
generator revenue forecast. 
8 
 
 
9 
Q. 
How was the MFC revenue component developed? 
10 
A. 
The MFC surcharge, which is designed to recover gas supply-related costs, 
11 
was developed based on the New York Mercantile Exchange (“NYMEX”) 
12 
forward gas prices as of December 28, 2022.   
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please explain why the DCSM Long-Term Capital Capacity Projects 
15 
are a component of the Company’s Rate Year and Data Years revenue 
16 
forecast. 
17 
A. 
Pursuant to the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, the Company is 
18 
permitted to defer and recover the pre-tax weighted average cost of capital 
19 
(“WACC”) and depreciation expense associated with each of the Long-
20 
Term Capital Capacity Projects (identified in the Joint Proposal) placed in-
21 


--- Page 20 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 17 of 74 
 
service, through the DCSM based on certain conditions.  The revenue from 
1 
this surcharge is being included in the revenue forecast to offset the amount 
2 
of net utility plant and depreciation expense embedded in the Company’s 
3 
revenue requirement to present the actual increase in base delivery revenues 
4 
proposed in this rate case proceeding. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Please explain how the revenue forecast for the DCSM Long-Term 
7 
Capital Capacity Project component was developed. 
8 
A. 
The Company prepared the revenue requirement forecast for the twelve 
9 
months ending March 31, 2024 for the associated projects based on each 
10 
capital project’s actual net plant balance and associated depreciation 
11 
expense as of February 28, 2023.        
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please explain why the NUP Reconciliation Surcharge mechanism is a 
14 
component of the Company’s Rate Year and Data Years revenue 
15 
forecast. 
16 
A. 
Because the Company did not file for new delivery rates to be effective on 
17 
or before April 1, 2023, the NUP Reconciliation Surcharge mechanism is 
18 
converted to a two-way reconciliation through March 31, 2024 (capped at 
19 
the Companies’ capital forecast levels included in the 2019 KEDNY and 
20 
KEDLI Rate Cases for the twelve months ending March 2024). The 
21 


--- Page 21 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 18 of 74 
 
Company is authorized to recover the pre-tax revenue requirements 
1 
associated with the Company’s capital investments and associated 
2 
depreciation to the extent the actual revenue requirement exceeds the level 
3

V. 
Embedded Cost of Service Study 
4 
A. Purpose of ECOSS and Overview of Methodology 
5 
Q. 
What is an ECOSS and what is its purpose? 
6 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion a utility’s total revenue 
7 
requirement, including plant and other investments, operating expenses, 
8 
depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes served by the utility.  The 
9 
ECOSS computes, for each class, the return on rate base for the Rate Year 
10 
at present rates, and the total and incremental return on rate base for the 
11 
Rate Year at present rates, and the total and incremental revenue that must 
12 
be collected from that class to produce the system average rate of return on 
13 
rate base.  This information provides guidance in revenue allocation and in 
14 
the development of rates. 
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Please summarize the methodology employed for the ECOSS. 
17 
A. 
The ECOSS is prepared by analyzing each element of the utility’s revenue 
18 
requirement and assigning or allocating it among the rate classes.  The 
19 
ECOSS was performed using a proprietary model developed by HSG 
20 
Group.  This model uses the traditional three-step process as follows: 
21 


--- Page 26 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 23 of 74 
 
• Functionalization – Each of the Company’s costs and expenses, as 
1 
well as rate base components, are assigned or allocated among each 
2 
of the gas functions identified in Appendix A to the Commission’s 
3 
November 9, 2001 Order in Case 00-M-0504. 
4 
• Classification – Each functionalized cost element is separated into 
5 
demand, commodity, and customer cost categories. 
6 
• Class allocation – Each functionally classified cost element is 
7 
assigned or allocated among one or more of the Company’s rate 
8 
classes. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
Please describe the functionalization step of the ECOSS. 
11 
A. 
In the functionalization step, cost elements are separated among the utility’s 
12 
basic service functions by determining what physical purpose each cost 
13 
element serves. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
What are the functions included in the ECOSS? 
16 
A. 
The functions included in the ECOSS are: 
17 
• Supply and Storage – availability and supply of gas and storage to 
18 
meet seasonal and daily peak demands; 
19 
• Transmission – moves gas from supply and storage sources to 
20 
localized distribution facilities; 
21 


--- Page 27 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 24 of 74 
 
• Distribution – moves gas from the transmission system to 
1 
customers’ premises (includes service lines); 
2 
• Metering and Billing – connects customers to the system, measures 
3 
their usage and demand, and bills for the services provided; 
4 
• Collections;  
5 
• Sales Promotion – the Company does not promote gas sales and 
6 
therefore the cost associated with this function is zero; and  
7 
• Procurement. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Please describe the classification step of the ECOSS. 
10 
A. 
The Company’s gas distribution system is designed to meet three primary 
11 
objectives: 
12 
1. Connect customers to the Company’s distribution system; 
13 
2. Meet the aggregate peak design day capacity requirements of all 
14 
customers entitled to service on the peak day; and 
15 
3. Deliver natural gas commodity to customers, whether they are sales 
16 
or transportation customers. 
17 
 
Based on these objectives, each functionalized cost element is classified as 
18 
being customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-related, depending 
19 
on which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 28 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 25 of 74 
 
 
Cost elements classified as customer-related are incurred to attach a 
1 
customer to the distribution system, meter gas usage, and maintain the 
2 
customer’s account.  Customer-related cost elements are primarily a 
3 
function of the number of customers served and are incurred by the 
4 
Company whether or not an individual customer uses any gas.  Such costs 
5 
may include capital costs associated with the customer component of 
6 
distribution mains, as well as costs for services, meters and metering, 
7 
billing, customer service, and accounting and collection activities. 
8 
 
9 
 
Demand- or capacity-related cost elements are associated with plant that is 
10 
designed, installed, and operated to meet peak hourly or daily customer gas 
11 
flow requirements.  Demand-related components include transmission and 
12 
distribution mains, localized distribution facilities, and dedicated facilities 
13 
that are designed to satisfy individual customer maximum demands.  
14 
Demand-related cost elements are allocated among the classes based on 
15 
their contributions to the peak demand for which the system is designed. 
16 
 
17 
 
Cost elements classified as commodity-related generally vary with the 
18 
volume of gas sold or delivered (i.e., throughput) to customers.  Costs 
19 
related to obtaining gas supply are classified as commodity-related. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 29 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 26 of 74 
 
Q. 
How were costs functionalized to Supply-Storage classified? 
1 
A. 
The classification step for Supply-Storage separated those costs into costs 
2 
recovered through the GAC, and other costs related to supply and storage.  
3 
The amount of costs recovered through the GAC was equal to the GAC 
4 
revenue. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Please describe the process for determining how much of the 
7 
investment in mains should be considered customer-related versus 
8 
demand-related. 
9 
A. 
Distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the distribution 
10 
system (customer-related) as well as to provide capacity to meet customer 
11 
requirements on the design day (demand-related).  Therefore, the cost of 
12 
mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related.  
13 
The customer component was allocated among the customer classes based 
14 
on the number of customers.  The demand component was allocated among 
15 
the customer classes based on their contribution to design-day demand. 
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Please describe how the minimum-system study was performed. 
18 
A. 
Minimum-system studies are a widely accepted method to classify mains 
19 
between customer- and demand-related costs.  The customer-related 
20 
component is the portion of cost representing the least-cost system the 
21 


--- Page 30 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 27 of 74 
 
utility would install simply to connect customers, without regard to the need 
1 
to meet demand. 
2 
 
3 
The analysis begins by obtaining from plant and accounting records the cost 
4 
of mains the utility has installed in recent years, detailed by material 
5 
(plastic, steel, and cast iron), length, and diameter.  Then the installed cost 
6 
per foot is computed for each material/diameter type. 
7 
 
8 
The minimum system ratio is computed as the ratio of (X), the cost of 
9 
replacing the entire mains distribution system with the minimum 
10 
component, which is two-inch plastic, to (Y), the cost of replacing the entire 
11 
mains distribution system with plastic of the same diameter as installed. 
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please summarize the results of the minimum-system study. 
14 
A. 
For the most recent period, the minimum-system ratio was estimated to be 
15 
54.51 percent.  For purposes of the ECOSS, the Company averaged the 
16 
results of this study and the two prior studies, to promote stability and to 
17 
broaden the period of data used in the study. 
18 
 
19 
The resulting customer component of mains, which represents the portion 
20 
of cost needed to connect customers without regard to their design-day 
21 


--- Page 31 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 28 of 74 
 
demands (i.e., customer-related costs) was estimated to be 47.44 percent 
1 
and the demand component 52.56 percent. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Please explain the allocation step of the ECOSS. 
4 
A. 
In the allocation phase of the ECOSS, the cost elements that have been 
5 
functionalized and classified are allocated among the service classes.  There 
6 
are two types of allocation factors, or allocators, that are used for this 
7 
purpose: external allocators and internal allocators.  External allocators are 
8 
based on special studies derived from data in the Company’s accounting 
9 
and other records.  For example, the number of customers by service class 
10 
is an external allocator that was used in the Company’s ECOSS to allocate 
11 
some of the customer care costs.  Other examples of external allocators 
12 
include annual deliveries, design day requirements, and historic bad debt 
13 
experience.  Internal allocators are based on some combination of external 
14 
allocators, costs that are directly assigned, and other internal allocators.  For 
15 
example, the allocator for property insurance expense is based on plant 
16 
investment assigned to each service class; therefore, it is necessary to 
17 
compute plant investment by service class before property insurance costs 
18 
can be allocated among the classes. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 32 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 29 of 74

3

4 
below.

B. Revenue Allocation 
13 
Q.  
Please summarize the methodology used to develop the Company’s 
14 
revenue allocation. 
15 
A. 
In developing the Company’s proposed revenue allocation, the Panel 
16 
considered the costs to provide the type and quality of service required by 
17 
each service class as determined in the ECOSS.  The proposed revenue 
18 
allocation is intended to produce revenue from each service class that will 
19 
move the service class rate of return closer to the overall rate of return that 
20 
the Company is requesting, a concept known as “unity,” while mitigating 
21 


--- Page 38 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 35 of 74 
 
extreme impacts on customer groups, a concept known as “gradualism.” 
1 
 
2 
As presented in the testimony of KEDLI’s Revenue Requirements Panel, 
3 
the Company’s revenue requirement is $1,772.1 million ($1,738.9 million 
4 
without revenue taxes), representing an increase of $232.6 million ($228.2 
5 
million without revenue taxes) over revenue at present rates.  After 
6 
reflecting the effects of changes in other revenue items (MFC, Billing 
7 
Service Fees), the Company requires base delivery revenue of $1,119.5 
8 
million excluding revenue taxes, an increase of $226.1 million, representing 
9 
an increase of 25.3 percent.  Please refer to Exhibit __ (RDP-4), Schedule 
10 
2, page 1 for details. 
11 
 
12 
The tentative allocation of the overall delivery revenue increase of $226.1 
13 
million, and the development of class revenue targets, is presented on 
14 
Exhibit __ (RDP-4), Schedule 1 and the final revenue allocation to reflect 
15 
additional Low-Income Discounts is on Schedule 7.  The inclusion of the 
16 
additional Low-Income Discounts is a reallocation of the incremental 
17 
discounts between the service classes and does not represent an additional 
18 
overall delivery increase.  Therefore, the increase over pro forma base 
19 
delivery revenue at present rates remains at 25.3 percent.  Pro forma 
20 
delivery revenue equals delivery revenue based on forecast customer count 
21 


--- Page 39 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 36 of 74 
 
and volume at present rates (line 1), adjusted to reflect the elimination of 
1 
NUP and DCSM surcharges (line 2). 
2 
 
3 
To allocate the increase among the rate classes, the Panel employed the 
4 
same methodology as in past cases where class increases are guided by the 
5 
class returns relative to the system average return.  The average rate of 
6 
return on rate base at present rates is 3.55 percent (line 11).  A tolerance 
7

11 
and 1.35 times the average on the high end, or returns of 2.31 percent to 
12 
4.79 percent.  The only class within the tolerance band, SC1B, was assigned 
13 
a revenue target increase of 26.5 percent, slightly above the average 
14 
increase). 
15 
 
16 
Classes below the band (SC1A, SC1-DG, SC3B and SC17) were assigned 
17 
revenue target increases of 32.0 percent, a larger than average increase. 
18 
 
19

SC15), High (SC3A and SC16) and Very High (SC2A, SC9 and SC18 Non-

Firm Demand Response).  Over classes were assigned increases less than

C. Rate Design 
8 
Q.  
What considerations were used in developing the Company’s proposed 
9 
rates? 
10 
A. 
The Panel considered the following objectives in developing the proposed 
11 
rates: 
12 
• To collect the revenue target established for each service class in the 
13 
revenue allocation process. 
14 
• To avoid severely disproportionate impacts on customer subgroups 
15 
within a class. 
16 
• To provide signals to customers to reflect the effects of their usage 
17 
on the overall system, including supporting conservation.  This is 
18 
supported by increasing, where feasible, the tail block by a greater 
19 
percentage than the mid-block, thus moving away from a declining 
20 
rate structure.

VIII. New York Facilities System 
1 
Q. 
Please describe the NYFS. 
2 
A.  
The NYFS is a high-pressure gas transmission system that spans the 
3 
service territories of KEDNY, KEDLI, and Con Edison (collectively, the 
4 
“NYFS Companies”) and interconnects the NYFS Companies with the 
5 
interstate pipelines that serve the New York metropolitan region.  Gas 
6 
received into the NYFS from the interstate pipelines is delivered directly, 
7 
and/or by displacement, to the NYFS Companies.  The carrying costs and 
8 
O&M costs associated with the NYFS (“NYFS costs”) are allocated among 
9 
the NYFS Companies pursuant to the NYFS Agreement. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
How does the Company currently recover NYFS costs from customers? 
12 
A.  
Currently, the Company’s share of NYFS costs are included in the revenue 
13 
requirement and recovered in firm delivery rates.  In accordance with the 
14 
“Order Regarding NYFS Agreement” issued October 18, 2018 in Case 18-
15 
G-0318, the Company reconciles actual costs to the amounts included in 
16 
base rates.  Any over or under recoveries are included in the NYFS 
17 
surcharge mechanism included on the Statement of NYFS Surcharge.  
18 
 
19 


--- Page 50 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI)

the preceding block rates.

5

6

XV. 
Non-Firm Demand Response 
11 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s proposal for a NFDR gas supply cost 
12

13 
A. 
In accordance with the Joint Proposal in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate 
14 
Cases, the Company is required to develop and propose a NFDR gas cost 
15 
reconciliation mechanism to be included in this base rate filing.  The 
16 
Company has a combined Firm and Non-Firm gas supply portfolio 
17 
(KEDNY and KEDLI) and cannot separately reconcile NFDR customers 
18 
gas supply costs. Therefore, the Company is proposing to include the gas 
19 
supply costs incurred to serve NFDR sales customers and their revenues in 
20 
its annual GAC reconciliation excluding NFDR penalties.  
21 


--- Page 61 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 58 of 74 
 
 
Currently, the annual GAC reconciliation, makes an adjustment to exclude 
1 
the NFDR revenues from the actual purchase gas expense.  The difference 
2 
between the total adjusted GAC revenue and the total purchased gas 
3 
expense represents the GAC year over/under collection.  The over/under 
4 
collection is then divided by firm customer annual sales to derive the annual 
5 
cost of gas imbalance surcharge or refund and shown on the Statement of 
6 
Monthly Cost of Gas and Adjustments (“GAC Statement”).  
7 
 
8 
The Company is proposing to include NFDR revenues – discontinuing the 
9 
current process of removing the NFDR revenues from the actual purchase 
10 
gas expense – in its annual GAC reconciliation filing.  NFDR penalties will 
11 
be removed from the annual GAC reconciliation filing and separately 
12 
reconciled on an annual basis based on the GAC year.  The over/under 
13 
collection from both firm and NDFR sales will be calculated and refunded 
14 
or surcharged to firm and NFDR customers through a volumetric rate 
15 
included on the GAC statement for firm customers and the NFDR Statement 
16 
for the NFDR customers.  NFDR penalties will be separately reconciled 
17 
each GAC year and included in the adjustment section of the GAC 
18 
statement through a volumetric rate.  Exhibit __ (RDP-13) shows an 
19 
illustrative NFDR Gas Cost Reconciliation as compared to the GAC 
20 
reconciliation included in the year ended 2022 annual filing.

XVIII. Gas Marginal Cost Study 
15 
Q. 
Please provide an overview of the Gas Marginal Cost Study (“MCS”). 
16 
A. 
The purpose of the MCS, presented in Exhibit __ (RDP-9), is to compute 
17 
the incremental, or marginal, cost to the utility to provide the next unit of 
18 
service (i.e., the next dekatherm of design-day demand or the next customer 
19 
connected).  As shown on Exhibit __ (RDP-9), Schedule 1, line 10, the 
20 
Marginal Delivery Cost is $0.77 per annual dth.  Customers participating in 
21 


--- Page 76 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 73 of 74 
 
the Company’s Excelsior Jobs Program (“EJP”) will pay the marginal 
1 
delivery cost rate for all gas consumption in excess of the consumption 
2 
included in the applicable minimum charge.  The EJP rates are shown on 
3 
Exhibit __ (RDP-9), Schedule 1A.  Because NE:NY program costs are in 
4 
base rates but not included in the EJP rates, EJP customers will be charged 
5 
an energy efficiency program rate in addition to the marginal rate so that 
6 
they continue to be eligible to participate in Company-sponsored energy 
7 
efficiency programs. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
What are the components of marginal costs in the MCS? 
10 
A. 
The MCS includes the capital cost of the assets needed to serve an additional 
11 
unit of design-day demand, as well as the O&M costs related to the assets. 
12 
 
13 
The initial capital cost is developed by quantifying the relationship between 
14 
capital spending for growth, and the growth (additional dekatherms 
15 
delivered) supported.  The initial capital cost is converted to an annual cost, 
16 
representing the amount that would be included in the annual revenue 
17 
requirement to reflect return on rate base plus associated income tax, 
18 
depreciation expense, property tax and insurance. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 77 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 74 of 74 
 
In addition to the annualized capital cost and the associated O&M costs, the 
1 
marginal cost includes property tax and insurance costs related to the assets. 
2 
Marginal Demand Cost is stated in dollars per delivered dekatherm.  
3 
 
4

KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid NY 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The testimony of the Rate Design Panel describes the purpose of performing an Embedded Cost 
of Service Study (“ECOSS”), and summarizes the methodology used to prepare the ECOSS in 
this proceeding.  The testimony describes the three-step ECOSS process (functionalization, 
classification, class allocation) used to analyze each element of the revenue requirement, in order 
to assign or allocate it among the rate classes. 
This Schedule 9 describes the ECOSS methodology in more detail.  Part 1 describes the three-
step ECOSS process. 
Part II describes how each element of the revenue requirement- rate base, expense and revenue- 
was assigned or allocated in each of the three steps.  Plant, expenses and revenues are identified 
using the Uniform System of Accounts (FERC Accounts).  Part II serves as a guide when 
reviewing the other schedules in this exhibit. 
Part 1. DETAILED ECOSS METHODOLOGY 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion fairly a utility’s total revenue requirement, including 
plant and other investments, operating expenses, depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes 
served by the utility.  The ECOSS computes for each rate class the revenue to be collected in 
order to produce the overall required rate of return on rate base.  This information provides 
valuable guidance in revenue allocation, and in the development of rates, to recover the revenue 
requirement from all rate classes. 
The three steps of the ECOSS are: 
Functionalization- Cost elements are separated among the utility’s basic service 
functions, by determining what physical purpose each cost element serves.  KEDNY’s 
functions are: Gas Supply and Storage; Transmission; Distribution; Metering and Billing; 
Collections; Sales Promotion; and Procurement. 
Classification- Each functionalized cost elements is classified according as Customer-
related (connects customers to the distribution system); Demand-related (meets design 
day capacity requirements) or Commodity-related (Deliver gas commodity to customers). 
Class Allocation- Cost elements that have been functionalized and classified are allocated 
among the service classes, using an appropriate allocation factor for each cost element.  
Allocation factors can be external (e.g., number of customers, deliveries, design day 
requirements sales and historical bad debt experience) or internal (e.g., property 
insurance is based on plant investment).

Part 2. ALLOCATOR FOR EACH ELEMENT OF THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT 
A. Rate Base 
1. Intangible Plant (FERC Accounts 301-303) 
Primarily capitalized software costs for new and updated financial and operating 
systems.  Allocated in proportion to plant investment, based on a review of the 
applications that Intangible Plant comprises. 
2. LNG / Storage Plant (FERC Accounts 360-363) 
Assets needed to meet design day and seasonal requirements.  LNG and Storage plant 
are classified as Demand.  Storage is allocated based on seasonal (winter) requirements 
to all customers; LNG is allocated to all firm customers. 
3. Transmission Plant (FERC Accounts 365-368) 
Transmission plant moves natural gas from suppliers to the distribution system, and is 
sized to meet design day requirements.  Classified as Demand and allocated based on 
class design day requirements. 
4. Distribution Plant (FERC Accounts 374-386) 
Mains- Distribution mains connect customers to the distribution system (i.e., customer-
related) and provide capacity to meet design day customer requirements (i.e., demand-
related).  Therefor the cost of mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly 
demand-related. 
The minimum size main was determined to be 2-inch plastic.  For the most recent 
period, the minimum-system ratio was estimated to be 54.51 percent.  For the ECOSS, 
the Company averaged the results of this study and the two prior studies, to promote 
stability and to broaden the period of data used in the study.  The resulting customer 
component of mains, the portion of cost to connect customers without regard to design-
day demands (i.e., customer-related costs), was estimated to be 47.44 percent and the 
demand component 52.56 percent. 
The customer component was allocated among the classes based on the number of 
customers.  The demand component was allocated among the classes based on design-
day requirements. 
Non-Firm Mains- Additional costs incurred to connect Non-Firm Demand Response 
(formerly Temperature Controlled or Interruptible) customers were identified.  The 
portion representing mains extensions was directly assigned to the Non-Firm classes.

KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid NY 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Measuring & Regulating Equipment- Sized for design day operation, therefore 
classified as demand-related and allocated among the rate classes based on design-day 
requirements.  Industrial equipment is allocated among the non-residential classes. 
Services- Services connect the customer to the distribution mains.  There is a direct 
correspondence between number of customers and number of services1, therefore 
services are classified as customer-related.  The costs are allocated based on the current 
cost for a typical service line for each rate class. 
Meters- Meters (including installation costs and house regulators) are classified as 
customer-related, and allocated based on the current cost for a typical meter for each 
rate class. 
Land, Structures and Improvements and Other Distribution Plant- Allocated in 
proportion to all other Distribution Plant accounts. 
5. General Plant (FERC Accounts 389-399) 
Primarily Structures & improvements; Tools, shop & garage; and Office furniture and 
equipment.  General plant was functionalized, classified and class allocated in 
proportion to the direct labor content of operating and maintenance expense, because 
these assets primarily support direct labor. 
6. Depreciation Reserve (FERC Accounts 108 and 111) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
7. Other Rate Base Items 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
Materials & Supplies (which includes prepayments) and Cash Working Capital (non-
supply) were allocated in proportion to non-gas O&M costs.  Accumulated Deferred 
Income Tax and CWIP were allocated in proportion to plant in service.  Regulatory 
Assets and Earnings Base Adjustment were allocated in proportion to rate base.  
Storage Gas was allocated based on seasonal (winter) requirements.  Cash Working 
Capital (supply) was allocated in proportion to gas deliveries. 
B. Expenses 
1. Gas Costs (FERC Accounts 804-813)- Allocated in proportion to GAC revenue 
 
1 This is not a 1:1 correspondence; an adjustment is made for multiple-account premises.

2. LNG / Storage Plant O&M (FERC Accounts 840-849)- Allocated in proportion to 
LNG and / or Storage plant (as described above). 
3. Transmission O&M (FERC Accounts 850-867)- Allocated in proportion to 
Transmission plant (classified as Demand and allocated based on class design day 
requirements) 
4. Distribution O&M (FERC Accounts 870-894) 
Mains, Services, Meters, Regulating Equipment- Allocated on the same basis as the 
assets to which they relate. 
Operations Supervision & Engineering and Operations Supervision & Engineering- 
Allocated based on direct labor content of O&M accounts. 
Customer Installations and Other O&M - Allocated based on a special study to identify 
the activities reflected in each account. 
5. Customer Accounts Expenses (FERC Accounts 901-919) 
These accounts were functionalized among Collections, Billing and Distribution based 
on a study of competitive functions performed by the utility.  The accounts are all 
customer-related. 
Supervision (Account 901)- Allocated in proportion to Customer records and 
collections (Account 903). 
Meter reading (Account 902)- Allocated based on the investment in meters. 
Customer records and collections (Account 902)- Billing-related activities are Print 
and mail bills, and Bill calculation.  Collections-related activities are a portion of Call 
center, Credit & collections, Collections and Field Collections.  Distribution-related 
activities are the balance of Call center, Credit & collections, Collections, Field 
Collections and Payment processing as well as Postage outbound and Postage inbound. 
Each functionalized activity was allocated among the rate classes using an appropriate 
allocation factor, and the results were summed to compute allocators for Account 903- 
Distribution, Account 903- Billing and Account 903- Collections. 
Uncollectible accounts expense (Account 904)- Allocated based on historical write-off 
experience. 
Miscellaneous customer accounts (Account 905)- Activities are primarily customer 
contact; allocation based on number of customers.

Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Customer assistance expenses (Account 908) and Information & instructional (Account 
909)- Primarily costs for energy efficiency programs; allocated in proportion to firm 
delivery volumes. 
Demonstration & selling ( (Account  912) and Advertising (Account 913)-  Allocated 
based on Gas delivery volumes. 
6. Administrative & General expenses (FERC Accounts 920-939) are grouped as follows: 
 Most A&G expenses are labor-related, and are functionalized, classified and 
allocated in proportion to direct labor content of O&M accounts. 
 Plant-related expenses are functionalized, classified and allocated in proportion 
to according to gross plant. 
 Franchise requirements (Account 927) and Regulatory commission expense 
(Account 928) are functionalized to Distribution, classified as Demand and 
allocated based on Rate base. 
 Miscellaneous General Expenses were allocated based on firm deliveries. 
7. Depreciation and Amortization Expense (FERC Accounts 403-407) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
8. Taxes other than on income 
Property taxes were allocated in proportion to plant, excluding services and meters.  
Payroll taxes were allocated in proportion to direct labor content.  Other taxes were 
allocated in proportion to plant. 
9. Income Taxes 
Income Taxes were allocated in proportion to Pretax income. 
C. Revenue 
Revenue was functionalized and classified based on revenue requirements and 
allocated based on forecast revenue at present rates in the Historic Test Year. 
Rent from gas property was allocated based on design day demand, reflecting the 
assets that give rise to the revenue.  Late payment revenue was allocated based on 
historical write-off experience.  Billing to ESCOs, which is on a per-customer basis, 
was allocated based on number of customers.  Other Revenues were allocated based on 
gas deliveries.  Joint Facilities revenue was allocated based on design day 
requirements.
